Abraham Lincoln's second inauguration. On March 4, 1865, with Union victory nearly assured, Lincoln delivered an address of just 703 words, making it the shortest of any second-term inauguration in American history, yet one of the greatest political speeches ever delivered. Lincoln sought to explain the war's purpose and frame Reconstruction around reconciliation and charity toward the South. He presented the war as divine judgment upon the entire nation for the evil of slavery, transcending partisan blame and instead creating a shared moral responsibility. He introduced the phrase with firmness in the right, as God gives us to see the right, balancing moral clarity with humility. His most famous words offered a vision for peace: malice toward none, with charity for all. Lincoln refused to celebrate Northern triumph, instead urging mutual responsibility for healing the wounds of war. He emphasized forgiveness over punishment, seeking a path to reunion that could begin to bind the nation's terrible wounds. Barely six weeks later, on April 14, 1865, Lincoln was assassinated, making this address his final major public statement. His second inaugural address would outlast him, shaping how subsequent generations understood both the Civil War and the possibilities for reconciliation after national trauma.
